Good afternoon. Thank you all for coming. Look around this room — family, friends, neighbors, coworkers, people who knew Jason for fifty years and people who knew him for five. He would have been quietly astonished by this turnout, and then he would have made a joke to change the subject. So let's give him that moment. Let's be astonished together.

Jason left us last Tuesday, at Oakwood Medical Center. He was sixty-seven years old. Sixty-seven sounds like a number, but it isn't. It's a lifetime of mornings, of coffee cups, of phone calls, of hands fixing things that other people had given up on.

[pause]

I stood beside Jason for as long as I can remember — as his brother. We grew up in the same house, under the same roof, with the same rules and the same stubborn streak, and somehow we turned out different in every way except the ones that mattered. He was the one who told me the truth when I didn't want to hear it. He was the one who showed up without being asked. That's the whole of it, really. Jason showed up.

He wasn't a man of grand speeches. He was a man of small, constant acts. He remembered your birthday. He noticed when your car needed air in the tires. He asked about your kid by name, and then asked again the next time, because he'd actually listened the first time. If you needed a ride at an inconvenient hour, or a hand moving a couch up three flights of stairs, or someone to sit with you in a hospital hallway and say nothing at all — Jason was already putting on his jacket.

He worked hard, and he worked honestly, and he never once believed that was anything to brag about. To him, work was simply the price of being useful to the people he loved. He gave decades of himself to his job and to this community, and he did it the same way he did everything: without fanfare, without complaint, and with a quiet pride that you had to be paying attention to notice.

And oh, that sense of humor. Dry as a cracker. He could deliver a line so flatly that half the room would miss it — and then he'd catch your eye, and you'd both know. That look. If you ever got that look from Jason, you were in the club. You were family, whether or not there was blood involved.

[pause]

Here is what I want to say to those of you who are hurting most today. Grief is not a measure of how little faith we have. Grief is love with nowhere left to go. It is the bill that comes due on every real attachment we are lucky enough to make. So don't apologize for your tears, and don't rush them. Jason earned every one of them.

And he did not leave us empty-handed. He left us a way of living. Be the one who shows up. Do the unglamorous thing well. Call your brother. Fix what's broken. Tell the truth, kindly. Laugh at yourself. Keep your word. That is Jason's legacy — not a monument, but a set of habits, and every one of us in this room is capable of carrying them forward starting tomorrow morning.

Whatever you hold sacred — whether you call it God, or goodness, or simply the love that outlasts a body — I believe Jason is held in it now, whole and at peace, free of every ache and every worry he carried so quietly for our sake.

So this is not goodbye. It is the older, harder word: thank you. Thank you, Jason, for the rides and the repairs and the phone calls. For the terrible jokes and the steady hands. For being my brother — and for being, in the truest sense, a good man.

[pause]

When you leave here today, don't just leave. Find someone who loved him and tell them a story about him — the sillier the better. That is how he stays with us. Not in stone, but in the telling.

Rest well, Jason. We've got it from here. We'll try to do you proud.

Amen."}
